title: Chapter 3 — Letting Go
paragraphs: It is the hot season, and Julia is complaining. Goy's answer is the chapter's thesis: you can't change the heat — you have to tham jai. Make your heart. Acceptance, in Mae Jaeng, is not resignation; it is something you do.

The vocabulary of release is everywhere once she hears it: ploy, to let go; plong, to lay a burden down; yom rap, to accept; mai pen rai, never mind. The interviews fill with case studies — Aung laughing off a lost thousand-baht note, a schoolteacher releasing thirty thousand baht of office money, a head monk whose wallet flew off his motorbike, a flood, a swindle, a miscarriage. And a death: when Uncle Anurak crashed, it was Moh Bom the doctor who phoned Gaew in the night with the town's tenderest formula — tham jai dii dii na, make your heart well.

The ritual calendar itself teaches release. At Songkran, the new year, the siblings ride a pickup through walls of thrown water and pile sand into stupas at Wat Kung — monuments built to be washed away. At Loy Krathong, Sen and Gaew take Julia up the mountain to release paper lanterns into the dark, "to float away worries," while at the reservoir little leaf-boats carry the year's troubles downstream. When Mae Daeng falls ill for weeks, she takes the pharmacist Ban's pills and floats the spirit doctor Nan Jon's prescribed krathong — biomedicine and spirit practice in parallel, no contradiction felt.

Merit-making gets the same analysis. Mae Daeng walks Julia through the offerings at the wat on Buddha days; Chai stops to move a frog off the road. The efficacy, Gaew explains, is not in the object given but in the feeling of the giving — intention is the engine of merit, as it will turn out to be the engine of karma.

The chapter's second half turns to who must let go of what. Sen argues in the shop that Mae Jaeng's women are not the "hind legs of the elephant" but the front: households are matrilocal (Pan, like most husbands, moved in with his wife's family), the market is women's, and yet the Sangha will not ordain them. Kreng jai — the deferential heart — keeps Sen from burdening his mother with his troubles, which means no one may raise them at all.

Even the self is held loosely. On their mother's instruction, Gaew and Sen change their legal names — to Wattana, "prosperity," and Monkut, "crown" — to turn the family's luck. Goy closes the chapter with her hot-room lesson: the room doesn't make you suffer; wanting it cooler does. Tham jai and anicca, she tells Julia, are the same teaching.
